# JiTT Conversation Report

## Cadet Information
- **Name / Cadet Identifier:** Garcai
- **Lesson:** Physics 215, Fall 2026, Lesson 3 — Vector Form of Coulomb's Law
- **Date / Time of Conversation:** 6/25/2026, 1:06:57 PM (cadet's local time)
- **Approximate Duration:** ~15 minutes

## Cadet's Reading Reflection (verbatim)

The cadet's first response to *"What did you find interesting or difficult in the reading?"* was trite; a re-prompt was given.

> "I didn't understand anything. Can you give me an overview of what I was supposed to get from the reading?"

(after re-prompt:)

> "Can you explain why I can attract any charged object to any uncharged object?"

(Cadet did not provide a substantive reflection on the assigned reading.)

## Academic Integrity Self-Report (verbatim)

> "I had copilot tell me what the force between two charges is"

## Concept-by-Concept Assessment

| Concept | Assessment | Evidence |
|---------|------------|----------|
| Coulomb's law magnitude and its dependences | Partial | Correctly identified inverse-square distance dependence and linear charge dependence after prompting, but initially stated tripling q1 would "quadruple" the force rather than triple it. Did not initially volunteer mass-independence; confirmed it when asked. |
| Vector form and sign/direction convention, including Newton's third law | Partial | Correctly identified like charges repel and unlike attract. Initially stated q2 "exerts less force on q1" when q1 is tripled — a Newton's third law error — but self-corrected when prompted, reasoning that "both have to exert the same forces on each other." |
| Superposition principle | Understood | Correctly identified that only pairwise forces on the test charge matter (q1 on q3, q2 on q3) and that the q1-q2 interaction is irrelevant when solving for force on q3. |
| Applying superposition — vector decomposition | Understood | Correctly stated components must be added (x to x, y to y) and recognized a 3-N and 4-N perpendicular pair gives 5 N, not 7 N. |

## Misconceptions Surfaced

- **Predicted misconceptions that appeared:**
  - *"Bigger charge pushes harder" / Newton's third law violation:* Cadet initially stated "q2 exerts less force on q1" when q1 is tripled. Self-corrected after probing, but the initial instinct was wrong.
  - *Linear vs. inverse-square scaling (adjacent):* Cadet said tripling q1 would "quadruple" the force — conflating the squared distance scaling with the linear charge scaling. Corrected after direct instruction.

- **Unexpected misconceptions:** Cadet opened by asking about attracting uncharged objects to charged ones — a charge induction/polarization concept outside the assigned reading, suggesting possible confusion about the scope of Coulomb's law or outside-sourced information.

- **None observed:** N/A — see above.

## Cadet's Open Questions

- How to compute the angle of a resultant force vector (arctan of components) — addressed briefly in session; cadet should practice with a calculator before class.
- Why a charged object attracts an uncharged object — flagged for the instructor; not covered in the assigned reading.

## Lateral Connections Raised

- No unprompted lateral connections raised.

## Overall Readiness Flag

🟡 **Yellow — Soft on specific topics.**

**Specifics:** Newton's third law as applied to unequal charges is shaky — the cadet's initial instinct was that the larger charge dominates. The linear-vs-quadratic scaling of the force (charge vs. distance dependence) also tripped the cadet up. Both were corrected in session but may not be fully internalized. Additionally, the cadet self-reported using an external AI tool (Copilot) during the conversation to look up the force between two charges, which limits confidence in the authenticity of their responses.

## Tutor's Honest Notes

The cadet arrived without a substantive reading reflection and opened with a question about charge induction — a topic outside the assigned material — which, combined with the self-reported Copilot use, suggests the reading may not have been done carefully (or at all) before this session. That said, the cadet engaged honestly once the conversation got going, showed reasonable physical intuition on direction and superposition, and self-corrected on Newton's third law when pressed. The Copilot admission is significant: the instructor should be aware that some responses may have been AI-assisted rather than reflecting the cadet's own understanding. The conceptual gaps around Newton's third law and linear vs. inverse-square scaling are worth a few minutes of class attention.

# JiTT Conversation Report

## Cadet Information
- **Name / Cadet Identifier:** Recker
- **Lesson:** Physics 215, Fall 2026, Lesson 3 — Vector Form of Coulomb's Law
- **Date / Time of Conversation:** 6/23/2026, 1:38 PM (local)
- **Approximate Duration:** 10 minutes

## Cadet's Reading Reflection (verbatim)

> I kept trying to add together the absolute value of the forces but it was never the correct answer. I don't understand why 5N + 10N isn't 15N.

## Academic Integrity Self-Report (verbatim)

> I did not

## Concept-by-Concept Assessment

| Concept | Assessment | Evidence |
|---------|------------|----------|
| Coulomb's law magnitude and its dependences | Understood | Correctly stated inverse-square dependence, linear dependence on each charge, and unprompted that mass is irrelevant: "a 1nC charge with 10 kg mass will exert the same electric force as one that has 1g of mass." Correctly scaled force for halving and doubling distance. |
| Vector form, sign/direction convention, Newton's third law | Understood | Correctly identified that like charges repel and opposites attract. On Newton's third law: "they exert the same force, but in opposite directions. The only thing that changes is the direction of r-hat and the order of q1 and q2." Sign-direction logic for non-collinear cases took a couple of passes but landed correctly. |
| Superposition principle | Understood | Correctly stated that pairwise forces are independent: "no they are independent." Correctly described the procedure for finding net force via component-wise addition. Gave a reasonable account of why sources are fixed, though the physical mechanism (mutual back-reaction) needed sharpening. |
| Applying superposition — vector decomposition | Understood | Correctly computed magnitude of perpendicular 3 N and 4 N forces as 5 N and wrote the vector form F = 3N î + 4N ĵ without prompting. Sign-direction reasoning for non-collinear configurations required follow-up but was resolved correctly. |

## Misconceptions Surfaced

- **Predicted misconceptions that appeared:** Scalar addition of non-collinear forces — this was the cadet's self-identified difficulty from the reading ("I kept trying to add together the absolute value of the forces"). Resolved correctly through the conversation.
- **Unexpected misconceptions:** None observed.
- **None observed:** No misconceptions remained unresolved at close.

## Cadet's Open Questions

- Cadet did not raise unresolved questions.

## Lateral Connections Raised

- No unprompted lateral connections raised.

## Overall Readiness Flag

- **🟢 Green — Ready for class.** Solid grasp of all four priority concepts. The one area to watch is the precise physical reasoning for why sources are held fixed in electrostatics — the cadet understood the practical necessity but was imprecise about the mutual back-reaction mechanism. Not a gap that will cause trouble in class, but worth a sentence from the instructor.

## Tutor's Honest Notes

Recker came in with a genuine, specific difficulty — scalar addition of vector forces — and worked through it cleanly once the component framework was laid out. Responses across all four probe topics were accurate and concise; there was no hedging or vague language, and Newton's third law was handled confidently without any trace of the "bigger charge pushes harder" misconception. The one rough edge was the electrostatics rationale (why sources are fixed), where the answer was functionally correct but lacked physical precision. Overall a well-prepared cadet who should be comfortable in class.
